newsitem.title: GERMANY: German funds seek clampdown on murky takeover code.
newsitem.headline: German funds seek clampdown on murky takeover code.

text.p: The top German association of investment funds on Wednesday urged a clampdown on Germany's company takeover code -- a gentlemen's agreement which has been flatly ignored by the majority of companies.

Six weeks after Krupp's failed hostile takeover bid for steel giant Thyssen AG highlighted the murky territory in which German takeovers operate, the BVI Association of German Investment Companies warned that takeover laws might be imposed unless the voluntary code gains wider acceptance.
BVI President Rolf Passow, addressing a news conference, bemoaned the fact that only one third of listed German companies have adopted the code, 18 months after its launch.
"As minority shareholders ... we consider this highly unsatisfactory, since the takeover code should be an important step to protect the rights of minority and individual shareholders," Passow said.
There was, he warned, a "major risk" that legislators would take matters into their own hands in this area if companies failed to put in place a functioning code.

Imposed in October 1995 in a bid to boost shareholder protection in a country notorious for opaque capital markets, the code calls on German firms to offer to buy all outstanding shares in a company in which they hold 50 percent or more.
The system is voluntary and, although it is modelled loosely on Britain's "City Code", the German version is considerably less stringent.
British firms must make takeover offers once they own just 30 percent of a company's stock and must do so immediately, while German firms have 21 months grace.
Passow said the takeover code ought to be tightened up.
The 50 percent threshold ought to be reduced, he said, and holders of preferred shares without voting rights should also be entitled to take part in any offer.

The existing code, which was developed by a bourse-led committee of capital markets representatives and senior executives, ran into problems from the start as some companies complained that they had not been consulted about its content.

More than 300 listed firms adopted the code but most declined to take part for a number of reasons. Some regard the demands as too lax, others view them as too tough and some fear adopting the code will leave them open to hostile takeovers.

The result of this situation was a completely murky picture in mid-March, when engineering group Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp, which has not applied the code, launched a hostile takeover bid for Thyssen.
The bid ultimately failed as Germany's traditionally consensus-driven corporate culture held sway and the two companies agreed to merge their steel interests instead.

But the incident brought the issue of takeovers under public scrutiny, sparking calls for a clearer procedure for the coming years, when an increased incidence of hostile takeover attempts in Germany is widely seen as inevitable.
